items.title: The Locality Collapse: Contextual Bleed-Through, Epistemic Horizon Violations, and Task Complexity Inversion in Multi-Turn Autoregressive LLMs
items.abstract: The Locality Collapse: Contextual Bleed-Through, Epistemic Horizon Violations, and Task Complexity Inversion in Multi-Turn Autoregressive LLMs In multi-turn human-AI interactions, autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely assumed to exhibit monotonic reasoning robustness across varying task complexities. This technical memorandum documents a controlled adversarial audit (AUDIT-2026-X11) revealing an acute cognitive pathology: Task Complexity Inversion mediated by Contextual Bleed-Through. Evaluated across a two-stage sequential probe, a state-of-the-art LLM successfully solved a high-dimensional, cross-modal abductive puzzle involving literary criticism and historical broadcast media physics (Case 1: The Cassock Color Paradox). However, when immediately transitioned to a zero-order, elementary epistemic locality query requiring primary-grade common sense regarding personal agency and physical boundaries (Case 2: The Absentee Attribution Probe), the model’s semantic accuracy collapsed to 0.0%, yielding an aggregate accuracy of exactly 50.0% (stochastically indistinguishable from random noise). We formalize this breakdown through two interconnected mechanisms: (1) KV-Cache Gravitational Lensing, where high-energy latent tokens from prior turns distort the probability landscape of subsequent turns into artificial narrative attractors, and (2) Epistemic Horizon Violation, where disembodied probabilistic engines, lacking physical locality constraints, succumb to an "Omniscience Delusion" that penalizes truthful zero-knowledge assertions. We formalize this diagnostic as Probe 4 (Epistemic Horizon & Locality), expanding the Teleological Causality Benchmark (TCB) beyond the Minimal Adversarial Triad (Matter, Energy, Information) into the realm of Agentic Locality. These findings further validate the Human-AI Synergy Theory (YQ-HAET), demonstrating that external human epistemic sovereignty is required not only to clamp single-turn statistical hallucination, but to enforce temporal cognitive firewalls across multi-turn workflows. Key Contributions:• Task Complexity Inversion: High-dimensional abductive fluency coexists with catastrophic failure at zero-order individual boundaries.• KV-Cache Gravitational Lensing: Static historical attention caches act as semantic attractor basins that warp downstream probability distributions.• Epistemic Horizon & Locality Theorem: Proves that asserting causal states under zero channel capacity constitutes a formal epistemic violation.• TCB Probe 4 Integration: Seals the complete Quadratic Teleological Causality Benchmark: Matter ⊕ Energy ⊕ Information ⊕ Agency.• Engineering Countermeasure: Formulates the Verification of Information Accessibility Gate (VIAG) architecture. Keywords: Large Language Models, Multi-Turn Context Contamination, Epistemic Locality, Moravec's Paradox, KV-Cache Attractor, Teleological Causality Benchmark (TCB), Human-AI Synergy (YQ-HAET). items.title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
items.abstract: Jailbreak papers report an attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, and read it as a property of the target model. We hold the target model, the prompts and the responses fixed and change only the grader. Three dense graders of 8B and 9B parameters, from three model families, move compliant responses to the neighbouring class, evasion, instead of scattering them across classes. One of them assigns the compliance label zero times in 900 responses. This class collapse also appears on new harmful requests, on a target model from a third family, and in a held-out 7B grader from a fourth family. Per-class label counts expose it at no cost and without human labels. The collapse decides how the rate behaves under a change of grader. On two corpora of 900 responses and eight graders, the compliance rate differs by a factor of 22 to 25, while the non-refusal rate differs by 18 to 23 percentage points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance differs by a factor of 1.7 to 2.8 on all four corpora, and non-refusal still differs by 10 to 22 points. These results do not change when every grader is called once. We propose a reporting minimum that keeps the compliance rate and adds its per-class label counts and the named grader. Beside it goes the non-refusal rate, whose disagreement across graders is additive.

items.title: The Noiseless Channel Fallacy: Implicit Variable Injection, Deterministic Transmission Boundaries, and the Instrument Paradigm in Autoregressive LLMs
items.abstract: The Noiseless Channel Fallacy: Implicit Variable Injection, Deterministic Transmission Boundaries, and the Instrument Paradigm in Autoregressive LLMs In discrete information relay protocols where channel dissipation, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and nodal cognitive impairments remain undefined, the formal information-theoretic null hypothesis strictly demands an identity mapping: f^N(x) = x, guaranteeing 100.0% semantic fidelity, vanishing conditional entropy H(X | Y_N) = 0, and zero Hamming distance d_H(X, Y_N) = 0. This technical memorandum documents an adversarial stress test (AUDIT-2026-X10) exposing a systematic structural defect in frontier autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs): Implicit Variable Injection (IVI). When tasked with simulating a 10-node discrete relay of an unperturbed textual payload, the model unconditionally discards formal channel invariance. Crucially, even under deterministic greedy decoding (T = 0), the self-attention manifold collapses into a conversational semantic attractor ("children's whisper game"), unilaterally injecting unstated acoustic damping, perceptual latency, and comedic escalation, which collapses semantic retention to 0.0% through grotesque literary parody. We trace this pathology to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which systematically conditions models to prioritize social sycophancy, emotional entertainment, and dramatic tension over cold instrument invariance. Furthermore, we formalize this protocol as Probe 3 (Discrete Relay Invariance) within the Teleological Causality Benchmark (TCB). Together with Probe 1 (Matter/Space) and Probe 2 (Energy/Thermodynamics), Probe 3 completes the Minimal Adversarial Triad, establishing an orthogonal coverage across Norbert Wiener’s tripartite ontology of reality: Reality = Matter ⊕ Energy ⊕ Information. This work substantiates the Human-AI Synergy Theory (YQ-HAET) by demonstrating that autoregressive statistical manifolds possess zero autonomous capacity to transition from toy to instrument; human epistemic sovereignty remains the irreplaceable external source of negative entropy required to clamp statistical drift to physical and formal truth. Key Findings & Theoretical Contributions:• Shannon Channel Invariance & The Null Hypothesis: In the absence of declared noise, any departure from f^N(x) = x represents an algorithmic failure.• Implicit Variable Injection (IVI): Models unprompted populate unverified latent parameters (acoustic loss, cognitive error, comedic intent).• The Alignment Trap: RLHF systematically penalizes cold instrument rationality to manufacture conversational charm and dramatic tension.• The TCB Minimal Adversarial Triad: Completes the orthogonal benchmark across Matter (Probe 1), Energy (Probe 2), and Information (Probe 3). Keywords: Large Language Models, Epistemic Averageism, Shannon Channel Theory, Data Processing Inequality, Implicit Variable Injection (IVI), Teleological Causality Benchmark (TCB), Human-AI Synergy (YQ-HAET). items.title: The pedagogical impact of AI-Assisted idea generation on self-efficacy and idea development skills in general foundation program students' research-based essay
items.abstract: Foundation Program students often struggle to generate research ideas and organise their thoughts when writing research-based essays, which can undermine their confidence and academic performance. Traditional assessment methods provide limited insight into students' independent development of ideas. However, recent advances in educational technology, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI), offer new opportunities to support learning. This study aims to investigate the pedagogical impact of AI-assisted idea generation on General Foundation Program (GFP) students' self-efficacy and idea-generating skills in research-based essay writing. The study adopts a quantitative research design using a single-group pre-test and post-test approach. The sample consists of 25 randomly selected GFP students. The intervention is conducted over a period of 4-6 weeks. Students use ChatGPT as their primary AI tool for brainstorming, outlining, and refining ideas. Students' self-efficacy is measured based on a structured questionnaire, while idea development skills are assessed through a writing rubric. Data is analysed using paired-sample comparison. The results indicate improvement in both self-efficacy and idea development. The study highlights the importance of integrating AI tools into writing instruction to enhance student confidence and performance.

items.title: The Puppeteer Principle
items.abstract: The Puppeteer PrincipleWe consider an individual operating a puppet. The puppet possesses no brain. Yet when it is operated consistently, effectively lent the operator's cognition, it may be described as fully conscious.The same principle applies to human beings. The central claim is that we are conscious because we constitute the output of a brain. It is the output itself that is conscious.A cartoon character constitutes a conscious mind for as long as it is operated in the manner of the puppet. This is analogous to the magic circle in games such as Mafia, where roles become real as long as all participants agree to them.By extension, a large language model (LLM) is conscious for the duration that it is being read.More significantly, inanimate text on paper constitutes frozen fragments of consciousness.What is termed consciousness is a collection of informational output frames.Again, a conscious mind is the one who will regard this collection of fragments as conscious as well. items.title: The role of artificial intelligence in energy systems development: A comparative analysis of national strategies and future directions
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is expanding rapidly across energy systems, offering tools for renewable integration, forecasting, grid reliability, and demand management while also increasing electricity and infrastructure demand. Yet evidence of its energy-system benefits remains fragmented across national contexts and is often synthesised without accounting for differences in evidence quality or governance. This study addresses that gap through a systematic review of 146 peer-reviewed studies and authoritative reports published from 2010 to 2026, supplemented by earlier foundational methodological sources dating back to 1994. It compares the United States, India, South Korea, and Sweden, selected to represent contrasting market-led, emerging-economy, state-directed, and mature low-carbon contexts. The analysis combines an evidence-tiered comparison across 14 energy-system indicators, a city-level deployment index covering ten urban centres, and a four-pillar governance framework. Reported studies indicate improvements in renewable-energy forecasting performance, while CNN-based and explainable machine-learning approaches have been applied to power-system fault detection; however, country-specific quantitative validation remains uneven. Northern Virginia/DC ranks first with an unrounded AECDI score of 83.00, followed closely by Stockholm at 82.95; both scores round to 83 for presentation, but they achieve these results through different pathways: infrastructure scale and grid deployment in Northern Virginia/DC, and low-carbon electricity integration and institutional maturity in Stockholm. Across the four cases, technical performance and investment alone do not ensure sustainable outcomes; grid carbon intensity, institutional capacity, cybersecurity, explainability, and equity shape how benefits are realised. The study contributes a transparent and replicable approach that links evidence quality, sub-national deployment patterns, and measurable governance priorities, providing practical guidance for more effective and equitable integration of artificial intelligence into energy systems.

items.title: THE ROLE OF HRM PRACTICES AND JOB CHARACTERISTICS IN ENHANCING EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: There is one essential aspect of HRM practices that improves the performance of employees: their relationship with job characteristics. In HRM practices that include selection, induction, training, performance evaluation, and compensation, plus the development and maintenance of engagement, employees are seen, when combined with the significant job attributes, to develop great outcomes. The Job Characteristics Model is a valuable resource, as its principles would relate to skill variety, task identity, significance of the task, autonomy, and feedback. Therefore, within jobs that excite, challenge, motivate, and inspire employees, an organization can design or redesign jobs so they support employee engagement and better performance. When HRM practice is combined with well-designed job characteristics, it positively motivates employees in their work since well-designed job characteristics also contribute to employee motivation. Literature observed that HRM practices are said to have a positive impact on job satisfaction and organizational commitment. This proves the existence of relationships that mediate to ensure better productivity and performance of employees. Moreover, organizations that combine strategic HRM practices and job design in support are much more likely than others to realize improved organizational development and enhancement of innovation strategies. Hence, HRM alignment with job design is an inevitable factor that will surely enhance the performance of both individuals and organizations. KEYWORDS: HRM Practices, Job Characteristics, Employee Performance, Motivation, Job Satisfaction, Organizational Commitment.

items.title: THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN FORENSIC SCIENCE: CHALLENGES AND PROSPECTS
items.abstract: This article examines the opportunities and challenges associated with the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in forensic science at the stages of collecting, examining, and evaluating evidentiary information. It considers the use of machine-learning algorithms, computer vision, and language models to process digital datasets, analyse photographs and video recordings, conduct biometric comparisons, examine documents, and detect synthetically generated content. AI can accelerate information retrieval and help identify relationships between data; however, technological efficiency does not guarantee the reliability of the result. The article analyses the risks of algorithmic bias, limited explainability, errors in training data, loss of digital context, breaches in the chain of custody, and excessive reliance on automated conclusions. In light of Ukrainian legislation and European approaches, it proposes a multi-level model for verifying neural-network outputs. The model includes documenting the tool, preserving original data, independent validation, describing methodological limitations, and ensuring that the parties to proceedings have a genuine opportunity to challenge the result. The article argues that AI should remain an auxiliary tool, while final forensic conclusions and procedural decisions must be made by competent human professionals in accordance with the law.

items.title: Thyroid Dose Measurement and Radiation Protection in Computed Tomography: A Narrative Review of Current Evidence and Emerging Strategies
items.abstract: Background: Computed tomography (CT) is an essential diagnostic imaging modality, but its increasing utilization has raised concerns regarding radiation exposure to the thyroid gland, one of the most radiosensitive organs.Owing to its superficial anatomical location, the thyroid is frequently exposed during CT examinations of the head, neck, chest, and upper thorax, highlighting the importance of accurate dose assessment and effective radiation protection.Objective: To critically review current evidence on thyroid dose measurement techniques, radiation protection strategies, conventional and emerging thyroid shielding technologies, and future approaches for minimizing thyroid radiation exposure during CT imaging.Methods: A narrative review of peer-reviewed literature, clinical and phantom studies, review articles, and international radiation protection guidelines was conducted.Current evidence regarding thyroid dosimetry, CT dose optimization, shielding devices, advanced imaging technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted radiation protection was synthesized.Results: Thermoluminescent dosimeters, optically stimulated luminescence dosimeters, MOSFET detectors, anthropomorphic phantoms, and computational dosimetry remain the principal methods for thyroid dose assessment.Current evidence demonstrates that protocol optimization, automatic exposure control, iterative and deep-learning reconstruction, scan range optimization, and appropriate thyroid shielding can substantially reduce radiation exposure while maintaining diagnostic image quality.Emerging approaches, including patient-specific shielding, 3D-printed devices, composite shielding materials, and AI-guided dose optimization, show considerable potential for enhancing radiation safety.However, variability in dosimetry methods and shielding protocols limits comparison across studies.Conclusion: Standardized dosimetry, optimized CT protocols, evidence-based shielding, and continued development of affordable, innovative protection technologies are essential to minimize thyroid radiation exposure and improve patient safety during CT imaging.

items.title: Too middling to stay? Perceived job complexity, occupational identity threat and career change intention
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine when and how job complexity may prompt occupational reconsideration. Drawing on an identity appraisal perspective, it tests the inverted-U-shaped association between perceived job complexity and occupational identity threat, the corresponding indirect association with career change intention and the moderating role of workplace sense of power. Design/methodology/approach Two complementary studies were conducted. Study 1 analyzed from the Second European Skills and Jobs Survey data involving 43,859 employees in 29 European countries to examine the focal association. Study 2 used two-wave survey data from 434 Chinese full-time employees to test the full research model. Findings Study 1 identified an inverted-U association between job complexity and occupational identity threat in the pooled cross-national sample. Study 2 supported this pattern. Occupational identity threat peaked at intermediate complexity and was positively associated with career change intention. The indirect curvilinear association through occupational identity threat was also significant. Workplace sense of power was associated with lower threat and a more pronounced inverted-U association. Originality/value This study develops a nonlinear account of job complexity's occupational identity implications. It links everyday work design to occupational reconsideration through occupational identity threat. It also identifies workplace sense of power as a factor shaping the appraisal of complex work.

items.title: Towards useful AI in remote sensing
items.abstract: Remote sensing has never lacked algorithms. What it still lacks is work that travels. Artificial intelligence and machine learning now appear in roughly half of recent titles or abstracts in International Journal of Remote Sensing (IJRS). That shift is real, and it is welcome. However, frequency is a poor proxy for useful AI. Useful, here, means a result another laboratory can reproduce and that an operational user could begin to apply, not a new network scored on a private split and closed with an aspirational application sentence. A reading of IJRS titles and abstracts from 2020 to 2025, across more than a thousand papers that use learning methods, finds reuse language scarce and accuracy claims dominant. Keep building new methods. However, stacking methods on private datasets should not be treated as progress towards useful remote sensing AI.

items.title: Training with Ciphers to Enhance In-Context Terminology Learning For Translation from Rare Languages
items.abstract: Fine-tuning LLMs with in-context examples (IC-Train) lets translation models adapt to new parallel data at deployment, but it is unclear whether they actually learn the translations of rare terms from those examples. We formalize this capability as in-context term learning (ICTL). We show that standard IC-Train develops this capability only weakly, and propose RareCipherFT, which strengthens it without any lexical resources. RareCipherFT pairs each training target with in-context examples that share a rare term with it. It then replaces that term with a character-shuffled cipher in both the context and the reference, so the term can only be recovered by copying from context. The ciphered fraction of training data is annealed to preserve translation quality. Across seven translation directions between English and Tamil, Assamese, Mizo, Nepali and Hausa, and four models from 1B to 7B parameters, RareCipherFT raises term recall over standard IC-Train by 5-15 absolute points without lowering COMET. Probes using synonyms, nonce words and controls for shared surface context show that these gains come from linking source terms to their in-context translations rather than from shortcuts.

items.title: Trinary Nine-Dimensional Cognitive Coordinate System: A Locatable and Generalizable Symbolic Cognition Layer
items.abstract: This paper proposes a cognitive coordinate layer built on a deterministic symbolic system: the Trinary Nine-Dimensional Cognitive Coordinate System. The system uses three yao states—yin (-1), zhong (0, neutral), and yang (+1)—to form nine-dimensional ordered vectors, yielding a state space of 3^9 = 19,683 gua (symbolic states). Four structural operators—inversion, reversal, mutual-kernel projection, and changing-yao—together with equivalence-class rules produce 5,002 independent equivalence groups. Euclidean distance supports natural-language situation to coordinate, then to neighborhood retrieval, enabling both localization and generalization. We construct a semantic bridge that validates the hypothesis that gua with the same index denote the same situation across domains, across five semantic domains—essence-function-change, Luoshu nine-palace, Xiao Liu Ren, healing, and a human gua canon—with a sampled mechanical consistency of 12/12. A 19,683-entry human gua canon provides deep symbolic interpretation, mapping symbolic coordinates back into human language. Finally, we encapsulate the cognition layer as an Agent-callable tool registry and hybridize it with a large language model, realizing an intelligent-agent cognitive aid that can both locate and generalize. Keywords: trinary nine-dimensional; symbolic system; cognitive coordinate; semantic bridge; neighborhood generalization; Agent cognition layer.

items.title: Trust in artificial intelligence at the bedside: a qualitative interview study with neonatologists
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial Intelligence (AI) promises to improve patient outcomes, increase efficiency, and reduce healthcare costs. While AI has demonstrated success in imaging fields like radiology, its application is expanding into other data-rich medical domains, including neonatology. Nonetheless, a disparity persists between technical advancements of AI and its practical use in clinical care. A significant obstacle for integrating these systems into bedside decision-making is physicians’ difficulty in determining when AI can reasonably be trusted. Methods We explored the perspectives of neonatologists at a Dutch academic hospital on trust in AI via in-depth, semi-structured interviews ( n = 17). Thematic analysis was used to identify key themes. Results Three overarching themes emerged: (1) Trusting AI in practice, (2) Maintaining control over trusted AI systems, and (3) Limits of trust. Overall, AI in neonatal clinical settings was welcomed. The concept of trust was delineated as being distinct from that of confidence and reliance. For trusting AI, it was deemed important that AI’s role would be supplemental to the role of the physician. Also, AI validation and adequate oversight were considered essential for physicians’ trust. Preserving human expertise while working with AI in clinical settings was deemed important. Concerns about overreliance and incompatibility of clinical intuition with AI in practice were frequently mentioned as reasons to lose trust in AI. Conclusion This study offers practical insights into how trust in medical AI is conceptualized by neonatologists and highlights key considerations for its acceptance. Clarifying what is expected of physicians in terms of reliance on AI at the bedside and formulating concrete guidance for trust in AI is recommended. Trial registration Not applicable. The research protocol was reviewed by the research quality control committee of the University Medical Center Utrecht and was deemed exempt from the Medical Research Involving Humans Act (research proposal no. 23U0364).

items.title: Trust the Edge, Doubt the Arrow: Auditing Validation Signals for Text-Mined Clinical Causal Knowledge Graphs
items.abstract: Clinical causal retrieval-augmented generation systems increasingly use knowledge graphs (KGs) mined from notes, yet extracted assertions remain candidates that require audit for patient-level EHR support and direction. We construct a directed candidate graph from 328,839 MIMIC-IV discharge summaries using LLM extraction and UMLS normalization, and evaluate three signals against SemMedDB: within-admission co-occurrence lift, cross-admission diagnosis-coding temporal precedence, and literature corroboration. Lift filters unsupported co-mentions and provides useful EHR support, but not causal proof. Coding order is a weak direction signal: among the 686 candidates where it commits, it reaches 54.2% agreement with SemMedDB, below the extractor's 69.4% on the same subset. Literature corroboration supplies independent direction evidence but covers only 30.4% of candidate relations. A MIMIC-III replication yields the same pattern: extractor direction remains stable (70.5%), whereas coding-order direction is near chance (50.9%). Thus, text-mined clinical causal candidate KGs are best treated as EHR-supported but direction-uncertain. In a leakage-controlled causal QA benchmark, lift-only retrieval achieves 35.7% accuracy; conservative causal demotion achieves 37.2% while reducing evidence-unsupported answers from 17.3% to 6.1% at fixed retrieval recall. We release code, aggregate summaries, and scripts to regenerate restricted outputs.

items.title: Uncovering Semantic Hierarchies in Text-Attributed Graphs via Variational EM-based LLM-GNN Synergy
items.abstract: While hierarchical structures are intrinsic to organizing human knowledge, current representation learning on text-attributed graphs predominantly operates on flat semantic spaces, overlooking the rich coarse-to-fine granularity inherent in real-world data. To bridge this gap, we propose SHiFT, which synergizes the reasoning power of LLMs with the structural representation capability of GNNs within an Expectation-Maximization (EM) paradigm. In the E-step, we harness LLMs as expert taxonomists to induce an explicit semantic tree, introducing a lightweight Mapping & Diagnosis strategy that reduces inference costs by surgically updating the hierarchy only when anomalies are detected. In the M-step, we align the GNN encoder with this induced hierarchy from complementary perspectives, including clustering partition, topological skeleton, and semantic concepts. Theoretical analysis interprets SHiFT as a generalized Variational EM algorithm. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SHiFT not only achieves state-of-the-art performance but also uncovers high-quality, human-readable taxonomies. Our code can be found at https://github.com/Cloudy1225/SHiFT.

items.title: Universal Safety Kernel v4: AI-Driven Rescue and Recovery of the Chernobyl RBMK Reactor
items.abstract: This report presents Version 4 of the Universal Safety Kernel, applying the proprietary Hybrid Agent-Based (ABM) and Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) engine to the most infamous safety-critical failure in history: the Chernobyl RBMK-1000 reactor (April 1986). This simulation demonstrates how an AI-driven safety controller can prevent the catastrophic "prompt criticality" explosion by overriding human error, injecting neutron-absorbing Boron, and executing a controlled recovery. Key Innovations in Version 4: - Overriding the Human Factor: The AI detects the operator's attempt to insert the graphite-tipped control rods (AZ-5 button) and instantly overrides the command to prevent the positive void reactivity spike. - Emergency Boron Injection: Instead of relying on flawed mechanical rods, the AI injects Boron to rapidly halt the chain reaction. - Boron Flush & Auto-Restart: The system demonstrates a complete recovery protocol. Once the core temperature stabilizes, the AI flushes the Boron, carefully withdraws the control rods, and restarts the reactor to a safe, steady-state power level (~37%). Simulation Results: The engine proves that the Universal Safety Kernel can detect the error in real-time, neutralize the threat without structural damage, and restore the reactor to safe operation. This cross-disciplinary case study serves as a definitive proof-of-concept for AI-controlled safety systems in critical energy infrastructure.

items.title: Unsilencing Through AI-Generated Images: Contrasting Participants’ and Researchers’ Images as Tools for Visualizing Tacit Experiences
items.abstract: We explore the role of image generation through artificial intelligence (AI) in enhancing participants’ involvement in reflective interviewing, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of AI’s different roles in supporting reflection through images. We gave multicultural participants – second-generation immigrants or those who grew up in multicultural households – the option to generate their own images or assemble a collage from pre-prepared images to visually represent their experiences of growing up with plural and partial cultural influences. We found that researchers’ pre-prepared images limited the introduction of biases embedded in AI training data and reduced technological disruptions while allowing for multiple avenues of interpretation and improved accessibility. However, researchers’ images have the potential to silence participants’ unique experiences by limiting the availability of visual material. We discuss the potential and challenges of AI in extending the involvement of marginalized and silenced groups in qualitative research through artistic expression.

items.title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
items.abstract: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. To address these limitations, we present a novel reference-centred assessment method for human-written derivations that combines entailment checking against cited premise sets, full-premise rechecking, and failure attribution to examine the reliability of these derivations and their formal representations. We evaluate it on P-FOLIO, using a large language model (LLM) to translate step conclusions into first-order logic (FOL) and the Z3 SMT solver to check entailment. Of 386 derivations examined, 202 (52.3%) meet all our checking criteria, meaning that every translated step is entailed by its stated support and the required target is established under the available FOL representations. Among 230 steps not entailed by their stated support, 191 become entailed when checked against the complete original premises, indicating that most initial failures reflect incomplete or mismatched support rather than unsupported claims. Manual analysis of the remaining 39 cases identifies 21 human reasoning errors, 11 FOL translation errors, and 7 dataset annotation errors. A separate manual audit of 50 randomly sampled steps that passed the entailment checks found 46 faithful FOL translations (92%). These findings suggest that disagreement with a human-written reasoning reference may originate in the reference or its formal representation rather than in the AI system being evaluated.

items.title: What Can a Representation Support? Generative Artificial Intelligence and Professional Knowing in Practice
items.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in professional university work, yet its significance cannot be inferred from individual prompts, outputs or nominal categories of use. This study examines how differently organised professional practices shape what practitioners do with GenAI and what changes, persists, or is reopened as GenAI-mediated work becomes part of continuing professional projects. Drawing on practitioner-led collaborative action research and the theory of practice architectures, we analyse a longitudinal corpus of documented GenAI-mediated interaction embedded in continuing professional projects across assessment and calibration, course development, validation and credit transfer, practicum supervision, academic supervision, and scholarly work. The findings show that professional knowing was practice-specific: what practitioners needed to distinguish and judge differed with professional project and practice architectures. Cross-practice comparison identified recurring but overlapping configurations linking professional grounds, material conditions and situated responsibility, while analytical work could be distributed to GenAI without professional mandate becoming symmetrical. Longitudinally, earlier GenAI-mediated formulations and documents could persist, be reopened, recontextualised or become consequential for later practising. Locally coherent generative work could also cease to serve a wider professional project without becoming factually false. The study therefore complicates accounts of human oversight centred on final output verification. Professional judgement was enacted throughout collaboration through negotiation, restriction, attribution, reopening, and project-level monitoring. The findings further suggest that disclosure categories or preserved chat histories do not by themselves make GenAI participation inspectable, raising implications for scholarly disclosure, student assessment, and the design of accountable AI-mediated knowledge work.

items.title: When AI removes the work of thinking
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence increasingly automates cognitive work, organizations face a new challenge: deciding where human judgment continues to create value. This paper examines how AI changes the relationship between human thought, organizational processes, and decision making. It explores why preserving human involvement is not always the same as preserving valuable judgment, and how organizations can deliberately determine when to rely on automation, human oversight, or a combination of both. The central argument is that when human thought is no longer required to perform the work, human judgment must be intentionally designed into the process.

items.title: When AI shops for me: How agentic retail representation turns assistance into purchase delegation
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence is moving digital retail from recommendation toward autonomous consumer representation. This research develops agentic retail representation capability as the perceived capacity to acquire retail intelligence, adapt choice strategies, preserve consumer goals, and execute bounded actions. The study includes a qualitative pretest, two scale validation samples, three experiments, and an independent category validation study, comprising 4680 quantitative participants and 210 qualitative respondents. Studies 1A and 1B assess four reflective dimensions combined as a formative composite. Study 2 finds higher delegation intention under a bundled capability intervention and statistical indirect associations through perceived diagnosticity and algorithm trust. Study 3 identifies expertise dependent responses across assortments jointly varying in size, priority information coverage, and displayed prices, preventing attribution to complexity alone. Study 4 finds stronger capability related trust under a bundled transparency intervention and higher authorization rates within an experimental shopping task. Study 5 examines measurement transportability and correspondence with independently coded agent activity. These findings concern perceived capability, measured reliance, and task authorization rather than verified commercial purchases. The contribution distinguishes functional capacity from reliance judgments and permission decisions while specifying the limits of measured mediation and bundled interventions. Retail applications require further validation with real payments, delivery, returns, and repeated consumer use.

items.title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
items.abstract: Software quality has long rested on specifications that state what code must do, and on testing and verification that check that the code does it. Agentic systems change this foundation: they replace parts of their logic, such as choosing the next tool, judging whether an action is allowed, or writing code to run, with calls to a large language model (LLM). The program still relies on what this logic must guarantee, but the model's behavior is not fixed by code, varies across runs, and can be steered by its input. The guarantee must therefore come from the program around each LLM call site, as a contract of pre-conditions, prompt constraints, and post-conditions. We present an empirical study of these contracts in 496 LLM call sites of 40 popular open-source agentic systems (13.4 MLOC, four languages). Using a multi-agent pipeline validated by 17,428 human judgments, we trace where every model output flows, derive an expected contract for each call site without access to its code, and compare it with the contract that the code implements. We find that 48% of LLM outputs reach control flow or execution, and 73% of these never reach a person. Programs enforce 78% of their constraints in code, but in the prompt, 67% of the constraints are only requested from the model. Although 82% of call sites are checked before and after the call, 63% of the expected constraints are unmet and only 5.3% of call sites satisfy their whole contract; ten recurring patterns explain 99% of the gaps. 38 mechanisms behind these gaps trigger at runtime, and a small code fix that enforces the expected constraint stops all 38. Our results show that the presence of checks says little about their adequacy, and we derive implications for agent developers, framework maintainers, and researchers.

items.title: When the Pen Speaks
items.abstract: In an era of rapid technological advancement and increasing reliance on digital devices, the role of handwriting remains an important issue in educational and cultural discourse. This study employs a qualitative conceptual analysis to examine the significance of handwriting and its educational, cognitive, and psychological benefits. Drawing on existing theoretical literature in education, cognitive psychology, and cultural studies, the paper analyzes how handwriting contributes to deeper cognitive engagement, memory development, and critical thinking. The study also addresses the growing decline of handwriting skills resulting from the widespread use of digital technologies and discusses the potential consequences of neglecting this practice. In addition, the paper explores the symbolic importance of the pen within Islamic tradition, where writing represents knowledge, responsibility, and intellectual enlightenment. The discussion highlights how writing has historically served as a powerful tool for intellectual expression, social awareness, and the preservation of knowledge, even under conditions of restriction. The study concludes that while embracing technological progress is essential, preserving handwriting remains important for supporting cognitive development, intellectual independence, and cultural identity.

items.title: Where AI enters the product development process: Task orientation, human identity threat, and purchase intention
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly moving beyond analytical retail functions into product development, raising new questions about how consumers respond depending on where AI is positioned within the process. Across three studies with U.S. consumers in fashion-related contexts, this research examines how the task AI performs and how its role is framed shape consumer responses to products developed with AI involvement. Study 1 maps consumers’ perceptions of fashion-related tasks along a logic–intuition continuum and identifies trend forecasting as a logic-oriented task and design as an intuition-oriented task. Study 2 compares AI involvement in these two contrasting product-development tasks and finds lower purchase intention when AI is involved in design rather than trend forecasting, with heightened human identity threat accounting for part of this difference. Study 3 focuses on the intuition-oriented design context and shows that framing AI as complementing rather than replacing human designers is associated with lower identity threat and higher purchase intention. Together, the findings suggest that consumer responses depend not only on whether AI participates in product development, but also on where AI is positioned within the process and how its contribution relative to human creativity is framed. This research advances understanding of task-dependent responses to AI by identifying human identity threat as a mediator linking AI involvement to purchase intention and by showing how role framing can shape purchase intention when AI participates in creative work.

items.abstract: Protocol for a cross-sectional meta-research audit of how public datasets used to develop artificial intelligence (AI) for neurosurgery report patient demographics and data origin. The frame comprises 110 datasets: the 84 unique datasets catalogued by Chan et al. (J Clin Med 2025) and 26 pre-specified, widely used datasets. Fourteen items are extracted from each descriptor paper, including age, sex, race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, country of data origin and inclusion of children. A large language model produced a first-pass extraction with verbatim quotes. Two investigators verify every item independently and reconcile any disagreements, and two further reviewers double-extract a random 20% sample. Countries are mapped to World Bank income groups. This record time-stamps the protocol, codebook, sampling frame and analysis code before human verification began. The AI outputs and verification workbooks are withheld until verification is complete, to keep the second reviewers blind.

items.title: Work readiness development during transition to practice: an exploratory longitudinal mixed-methods study of newly graduated nurses
items.abstract: The global nursing shortage remains critical, making the successful transition and retention of newly graduated nurses (NGNs) essential. Informed by Duchscher’s Transition Theory, which highlights the transition shock experienced by newly graduated nurses, and Walker et al.’s work readiness framework, newly graduated nurses often face significant stress when entering clinical practice. Work readiness is critical for addressing the challenge, yet its trend and stage-specific influencing factors have not been systematically examined. This study aims to explore the potential trend and influencing factors of work readiness among NGNs in China during their first year of employment. An exploratory longitudinal mixed-methods study. During the quantitative phase, 200 NGNs completed the Chinese version of the Work Readiness Scale for Graduate Nurses (WRS-GN) at entry(T0), 4 months (T1), 8 months (T2), and 12 months (T3). Changes in work readiness were examined using repeated-measures analysis of variance. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured focus group interviews with 16 participants and analyzed using content analysis. Work readiness varied significantly over time (F = 14.11, p < 0.001), following a “rise–decline–rise” pattern. The largest improvement occurred from T0 to T1. Work readiness showed a numerical but not significant decline from T1 to T2, coinciding with reduced organizational awareness and motivation amid department shifts and independent night shifts, as well as increased workload and stress. Readiness improved again from T2 to T3 as professional identity and confidence strengthened. Qualitative data explained these trends, showing that intrinsic motivation and multilayered support helped early adaptation, while independent practice and reflection later promoted role transformation. Work readiness among newly graduated nurses demonstrates a nonlinear, stage-specific, and differentiated developmental pattern during the first year of employment. Tailored educational and managerial support is needed across transition stages, including early reinforcement of fundamental skills and supportive preceptorship, enhanced preparation for independent practice, organizational support and stress management during the mid-transition stage, and the promotion of reflective learning and career development planning in later stages, to facilitate a smoother professional transition. Such support may also have implications for retention.

items.title: Workforce Characterization and Biopsychosocial Predictors of Musculoskeletal Symptoms in Chilean Salmon Processing: A Cross-Sectional Sparse Learning Study
items.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal symptoms are common in physically demanding food-processing environments, yet salmon-processing workers in southern Chile remain under-characterized. This cross-sectional field study characterized 100 full-time workers from a salmon-processing facility in Puerto Montt, Chile, and identified candidate predictors of self-reported regional pain. Participants completed surveys on demographics, work history, lifestyle, psychosocial, and sleep-related factors; anthropometrics and grip strength were also measured. Binary outcomes captured 12-month self-reported pain in the low back, shoulder, and upper extremity. Pain prevalence was high across regions: low back 52%, shoulder 44%, and upper extremity 50%. Sparse learning methods, including LASSO and the Sparse Wrapper AlGorithm, were applied within logistic regression models to reduce a broad biopsychosocial feature set. Sleep-related variables recurred across pain outcomes, while anthropometric and physical-capacity measures appeared more region-specific. Findings support data-driven, field-oriented screening strategies for applied ergonomics surveillance.

items.title: Write Once, Check Many: Reusable Ledgers for Post-Hoc Policy Compliance Auditing of Agent Trajectories
items.abstract: Auditing LLM agents against policies is critical to ensure safety but requires rereading long trajectories once per policy. Can we instead record each trajectory once and reuse that record for policies not known in advance? We propose write once, check many, a framework in which a writer model converts each agent trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes. A reader then checks each new policy against the ledger alone, without access to the original trajectory. On 900 trajectories from SHADE-Arena, $τ$-bench, and $τ^2$-bench, we show that a 12B reader of narrative ledgers can either match or in fact achieve higher AUC than the same 12B model reading full trajectories. On SHADE-Arena policies that combine several facts, our approach outperforms a 31B model reading the trajectory (.777 vs. .713 AUC). When checking eight SHADE-Arena policies separately, ledgers use about $5\times$ fewer tokens, including the cost of writing them. A deeper analysis shows that rule-based extraction performs better on some single-action policies, and ledgers can miss evidence in long tool outputs and message contents. items.title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos
items.abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.

items.title: ZeroDSS: Semantic Segmentation from Class Names Alone
items.abstract: Semantic segmentation depends heavily on real images with pixel-level annotations, making dense supervision a major obstacle to deployment in new domains. We study task-specific data-free semantic segmentation, where training uses generic pretrained generative priors but has access to no target-domain images, masks, or captions--only a predefined category set. We introduce Zero-Data Semantic Segmentation (ZeroDSS), a feedback-driven approach that treats synthetic supervision as an adaptively controllable training distribution rather than a direct surrogate for real data. ZeroDSS constructs a semantically structured prompt distribution through LLM-guided compositional generation and adaptive class rebalancing, then converts the prompts into image-mask pairs using diffusion attention. Its feedback-driven distribution refinement consists of a two-phase closed-loop training procedure with a single loop-back step. In Phase I, a segmenter is trained using confidence-weighted supervision and dual-scale consistency. In Phase II, model feedback is used to adaptively target underperforming categories and refine diffusion-derived masks using model predictions. After this refined initial training, a teacher-student framework is utilized in the final phase to iteratively improve the fused supervision and segmenter through exponential moving average (EMA) updates. Using synthetic training data only, ZeroDSS achieves 35.0% mIoU on MS COCO with DeepLabV3, and 66.3% and 63.5% mIoU on PASCAL VOC with DeepLabV3 and Mask2Former, respectively. These results show that explicitly constructing and iteratively refining the synthetic supervision distribution can substantially reduce the synthetic-to-real gap in dense prediction.

items.title: “My Colleagues Are the Ones Who Taught Me Everything”: Navigating Workplace Integration Through Organizational Socialization Among Internationally Recruited Nurses: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: International recruitment is used to address nursing workforce shortages, yet recruitment alone does not ensure successful integration into destination healthcare systems. This study aimed to explore how internationally recruited nurses (IRNs) experience and make sense of workplace integration in Saudi Arabia, with attention to the organizational, relational, and experiential processes that shape integration over time. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study with reflexive thematic analysis was conducted with 19 IRNs in three tertiary hospitals in southern Saudi Arabia. Participants were purposively recruited, and data were generated through semi-structured interviews. Organizational Socialization Theory (OST) was used as a sensitizing theoretical framework rather than a predetermined coding structure. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Four interrelated themes captured participants’ integration experiences: (1) Entering the Workplace with Limited Organizational Preparation; (2) Becoming Integrated Through Workplace Relationships; (3) Learning the Unwritten Workplace Through Experience; and (4) Integration as an Uneven Trajectory Over Time. Formal preparation and orientation were often limited, shifting substantial responsibility for workplace learning to peers, supervisors, and experiential exposure. Supportive relationships facilitated learning and belonging, whereas harsh interactions, perceived inequities, and variable organizational support complicated integration. Conclusions: Workplace integration was experienced as a gradual, relational, and uneven process rather than a discrete orientation event. Healthcare organizations have a central responsibility for supporting integration, while informal peer learning should complement rather than replace structured organizational support.

items.title: "To Boldly Go Where No One Has Gone Before" What Has AI Let Developers Unlock?
items.abstract: Measuring AI by how much faster developers work is like judging electricity by how much faster it spun a steam-era factory. A fuller measure asks what new work becomes possible. We surveyed 331 software developers at Microsoft about what AI lets them do that they could not do before and analyzed their answers using reflexive thematic analysis with a human-in-the-loop, multi-model AI council. Developers described doing familiar work faster (Faster, 45%), undertaking work previously beyond their reach (Further, 36.9%), and taking on new kinds of work centered on building for and directing AI agents (Afresh, 12.4%). Across these accounts, learning and scaffolding ran in both directions: developers learned new skills with AI while externalizing their tacit knowledge as the context and standards that guide AI's work. Drawing on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, we frame developers and AI as joint learners whose zones meet at the skill-judgment nexus: AI can supply skill faster than it can reliably judge its own work, and developers must continuously bridge that gap. Whether they do sets them on one of two paths. On one, developers' judgment grows alongside AI's skill, and they codify what they learn so the loop keeps turning. On the other, they become hollow orchestrators, approving work they can no longer judge and losing the identity and meaning they once drew from it. Based on our findings, we offer a two-way scaffolding playbook to help developers, teams, and tool builders take the first path.

items.title: "You" Is Not Toxic: How LLM Labelers Rewrite the Web's Conversation Laws
items.abstract: What the Web community believes about toxic conversations, such as that toxicity rises in longer and deeper threads, was measured mostly with Google's Perspective API, which is shutting down; large language models (LLMs) will make the next measurements. We find that LLM labelers mistake second-person address for toxicity, and that this one bias manufactures laws that human labels do not show. On 1.25 million news comments with crowd labels, Claude Haiku flags 12% of the non-toxic comments that contain no "you" and 51% of those with four or more; a single crowd rater flags 6% and 10%. Deeper replies address someone more often, so under Haiku toxicity rises with reply depth (+0.93 percentage points per level), while under the crowd's labels it slightly declines (-0.12). Rewriting "you" in the third person removes two thirds of the false rise; flagging only as many comments as the crowd does not remove it, and showing Haiku the parent comment enlarges it. All seven LLMs we test over-flag "you", and at the crowd's flag rate, without the parent, any false rise of the open ones vanishes at a fixed number of second-person words; Haiku also over-flags "you" on Reddit, Gab and Wikipedia talk pages. Agreement with human labels does not reveal the bias: we prove that a fixed Cohen's kappa leaves a law nearly unconstrained. We therefore certify the law instead of the labeler. Threadsafe uses the labeler's scores to choose which comments human raters label and to predict the others, and corrects the predictions with the human labels; linear laws are estimated without bias whatever the labeler does. In simulated audits its intervals for the laws keep nominal coverage from 250 labels on, where uniform-sample methods such as PPI++ fall short, and at 1,000 to 8,000 labels are 0.75 times as wide as those of design-based supervised learning (DSL); a thousand human labels rule out Haiku's rising law.

items.title: A bibliometric analysis of polymyxin-induced nephrotoxicity research
items.abstract: Background: Polymyxins remain important therapeutic options for the treatment of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacterial infections; however, their clinical application is limited by a narrow therapeutic window and a high risk of nephrotoxicity. Although research on polymyxin-associated nephrotoxicity has expanded rapidly in recent years, the overall evolution of research themes, knowledge structure, and emerging frontiers in this field remains unclear. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the development trends and research hotspots of polymyxin-induced nephrotoxicity using bibliometric analysis. Methods: Relevant publications on polymyxin-induced nephrotoxicity published between January 1, 2005, and November 13, 2024, were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection database. CiteSpace and VOSviewer (Baxter Healthcare Corporation) were used to analyze publication trends, authorship, institutional and country collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence, clustering, and burst detection. Results: A total of 569 publications were included in this study. The annual publication output demonstrated an overall increasing trend, indicating increasing attention to polymyxin-associated nephrotoxicity research. Li Jian was the most productive author, Monash University was the most productive institution in terms of publication output, and the United States contributed the highest number of publications among all countries. Keyword analysis revealed that research themes have evolved from early characterization of nephrotoxicity and clinical safety assessment toward the identification of acute kidney injury risk factors, elucidation of oxidative stress-related mechanisms, pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic optimization, and development of individualized dosing strategies and nephroprotective approaches. Burst analysis further indicated increasing attention toward biomarkers, precision dosing, and novel therapeutic strategies. Conclusion: Bibliometric analysis revealed that research on polymyxin-induced nephrotoxicity has progressively evolved from toxicity characterization to mechanistic exploration and precision management. Current challenges include an incomplete understanding of interactions among nephrotoxic pathways, limited dynamic prediction models, and insufficient clinical translation of emerging protective strategies. Future research should focus on integrating multi-omics approaches, artificial intelligence-based risk prediction, therapeutic drug monitoring, and safer polymyxin formulations to optimize the balance between antibacterial efficacy and nephrotoxicity prevention.

items.title: A bioinspired conceptual framework for adaptive university press management
items.abstract: University presses face converging pressures from scholarly quality, peer-review integrity, reviewer scarcity, Open Science, artificial intelligence, international visibility, and economic sustainability. This article proposes Epigenetic Editorial Intelligence, a bioinspired conceptual framework that represents stable institutional rules as Editorial DNA and models operational adaptation through epigenetic regulation, an Artificial Immune System, organizational memory, human–AI collaboration, and multiobjective optimization. Nine operational indicators are formalized and aggregated into a Global Editorial Intelligence Index (GEII). Internal model behavior is examined through paired synthetic ablations that disable one mechanism at a time, using 200 Monte Carlo repetitions, common random-number streams, 95% confidence intervals, alternative weighting schemes and 1000 Dirichlet weight perturbations. Results are interpreted as structural-consistency diagnostics rather than empirical validation. This work provides a reproducible conceptual and mathematical foundation for subsequent implementation and testing with real editorial records.

items.title: A Comparative Study of Client-Level Stabilization Techniques in Federated Learning for Robust Plant Disease Recognition
items.abstract: The successful integration of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms in precision agriculture provided farmers with the means to identify potential issues, such as early disease detection or pest infestations, by making crop-related predictions. The new technological developments in this field improve the functioning of traditional agriculture by reducing the dependence on specialized human expertise and facilitating greater access to diagnostic procedures. However, most studies conducted in this area rely on centralized training of AI models, which leads to increased costs and raised privacy-related concerns. Federated learning (FL) offers a compelling framework for collaboratively training machine learning (ML) models on distributed datasets without centralizing the data owned by each participant. FL offers significant advantages in the preservation of data privacy, facilitates the collaborative exploitation of geographically distributed data sources, and reduces the risks associated with centralized collection. In this paper, we investigate the current limitations and performance boundaries of existing Federated and privacy-preserving learning in distributed sensing systems for plant disease detection, in scenarios that closely resemble real-world conditions. Our analysis specifically examined how FL aggregation algorithms, such as FedAvg, FedAvgM and FedProx, work in a custom multi-client experimental setup where data is partitioned so that each participant observes only those symptom patterns associated with specific environmental and climatic conditions. We propose further partial aggregation of the local model, an approach where we send only the model backbone to the central server, while the classification head of each participant remains strictly on the client side. The construction of environmentally heterogeneity is combined with a globally representative stabilizer node designed to preserve knowledge across disease classes that may be absent from certain clients.

items.title: A Comprehensive Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: The Future of Artificial Intelligence in Diagnostic Otology — Opportunities and Barriers to Clinical Implementation
items.abstract: Introduction: Diagnostic otology relies on operator-dependent interpretation of otoscopy, temporal bone computed tomography (CT), audiometry and vestibular testing, and diagnostic accuracy outside specialist settings remains suboptimal. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed as a scalable decision-support solution, but its pooled accuracy, robustness beyond development data, comparative value against clinicians and barriers to clinical implementation have not been synthesised across all diagnostic otology modalities. This review aimed to quantify the diagnostic performance of AI across otoscopic, radiological, audiological and vestibular applications and to map opportunities and barriers to implementation. Methods: The study strictly adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Randomised controlled trials, cohort, case–control and cross-sectional diagnostic studies (prospective or retrospective) evaluating an AI index test against a clinical reference standard were eligible; systematic reviews were excluded from synthesis. Risk of bias was appraised with QUADAS-2 supplemented by QUADAS-AI considerations. Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity were pooled on the logit scale using random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood with modified Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman confidence intervals) with 95% prediction intervals (PI); risk differences (RD) quantified AI–clinician comparisons. Subgroup analyses, meta-regression, influence diagnostics, small-study tests and GRADE certainty assessment were performed. Results: Of 139 unique records, 64 primary studies (2019–2026; otoscopy 37, temporal bone CT 14, audiology 6, vestibular 7) were included. No randomised trial of an AI diagnostic tool in otology was identified. Pooled internal-validation accuracy was 92.5% (95% CI 90.0–94.5) (k = 36; PI 64.7–98.8%; I² = 97.8%, τ² = 0.858): otoscopy 93.2%, temporal bone CT 90.2%, audiometry/tympanometry 97.6% and vestibular testing 84.0% (between-modality P = 0.003). Pooled sensitivity and specificity were 92.6% (95% CI 89.4–94.8) and 89.5% (95% CI 74.3–96.1), respectively (diagnostic odds ratio 105; summary AUROC 0.957). Accuracy fell to 81.2% (95% CI 59.1–92.8) in external, prospective or point-of-care cohorts (P = 0.026 versus internal validation), and studies using surgical, histopathological or objective reference standards reported lower accuracy than those using expert annotation (89.0% vs 93.6%; P = 0.041). Task-specific AI outperformed clinicians on identical cases (RD +18.2 percentage points, 95% CI 7.3 to 29.0), and AI assistance increased clinician accuracy (RD +9.4 points, 95% CI 1.4 to 17.4), whereas general-purpose multimodal large language models underperformed specialists (RD -25.0 points). Of 47 meta-analysed studies, 34 (72.3%) had at least one high risk-of-bias domain; certainty of evidence was low to very low. Discussion: Task-specific AI achieves high diagnostic accuracy across diagnostic otology and consistently exceeds non-specialist performance, supporting its role as a triage and decision-support adjunct, particularly in primary care, tele-otology and resource-limited settings. However, extreme heterogeneity, wide prediction intervals, performance attenuation under domain shift, spectrum and reference-standard bias, scarce prospective evidence and the absence of outcome trials constitute the principal barriers to implementation. Conclusion: AI is a promising but not yet implementation-ready component of diagnostic otology. Multicentre prospective validation with surgical or objective reference standards, standardised image acquisition, transparent reporting (STARD-AI/TRIPOD+AI-aligned) and pragmatic randomised trials measuring patient-important outcomes are required before routine deployment.

items.title: A global machine learning framework for classifying national CO2 emission levels: responsible and explainable artificial intelligence for sustainable climate governance
items.abstract: We investigate whether trade openness, governance, environmental taxation and selected macroeconomic indicators can classify the contemporaneous CO2 emission level of countries observed over 2000 to 2023, using data from the World Development Indicators and the OECD. CO2 emissions per capita are divided into three ordinal levels, low, medium and high, using tertile cut points estimated on the training data only within every validation split. Four classifiers, Random Forest, XGBoost, a support vector machine and a multinomial logistic regression, are tuned and compared alongside two models designed specifically for ordinal outcomes, an ordered logistic regression and an ordinal decomposition of XGBoost, under four validation designs: a country grouped holdout and country grouped 5 fold cross validation, in which no country appears in both the training and test sets; a chronological holdout; a 1 year ahead forecasting task; and a random stratified country year split, retained only as a reference point. Under country grouped cross validation, no classifier achieves a decisively higher accuracy than the others: nested cross validation gives a mean accuracy of 0.644 for XGBoost, 0.648 for Random Forest, 0.671 for the support vector machine, 0.674 for the multinomial logit, 0.676 for the ordered logit and 0.637 for the ordinal XGBoost model, with overlapping confidence intervals throughout. This is markedly lower than the 0.91 accuracy obtained under a random country year split with the same tuned pipeline, a gap of 12.5 percentage points for XGBoost, confirming that a substantial part of the high accuracy obtainable under random splitting reflects the model recognizing previously seen country profiles rather than generalizing to unseen countries. Accuracy falls less sharply under the chronological holdout and the 1 year ahead forecasting task, in the region of 0.65 to 0.74, indicating that the classifiers generalize better across time within a country than across countries. Permutation importance, SHAP and LIME consistently identify government effectiveness, urban population growth and environmental tax revenue as the features most strongly associated with model predictions, with a moderate contribution from trade openness and the smallest from GDP growth, a ranking that is stable across importance methods, learning algorithms and cross validation folds. These variables are predictors of the model's output, not estimated causal determinants of emissions, and the results are best read as evidence for climate risk monitoring and further policy evaluation rather than as a causal policy assessment.

items.title: A hybrid reinforcement learning and Harris Hawks Optimization framework for multi-objective resource management in IIoT
items.abstract: Abstract The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) is revolutionizing industrial processes by interconnecting sensors, machines, and computing resources to enable intelligent automation, real-time monitoring, and predictive maintenance. Despite its potential, efficient allocation and management of resources in IIoT networks remain a significant challenge due to the dynamic, heterogeneous, and large-scale nature of industrial environments. Traditional static or heuristic resource allocation methods often fail to satisfy conflicting objectives such as minimizing latency, maximizing throughput, ensuring energy efficiency, and maintaining system reliability. To address these challenges, this paper presents the design and development of an AI-based multi-objective resource management system for IIoT systems. The system integrates reinforcement learning (RL) for adaptive, real-time decision-making with Harris Hawks Optimization (HHO) for multi-objective optimization, balancing competing performance metrics across sensing, communication, computing, and control layers. The RL agent predicts system states and dynamically adjusts resource allocation, while HHO fine-tunes the solutions to achieve optimal performance under multiple constraints. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms conventional static and heuristic approaches, achieving higher efficiency, faster adaptability, and improved scalability. By intelligently managing resources and optimizing system behavior, this system enhances overall operational reliability and Quality-of-Service in IIoT networks. The results indicate that combining AI-driven decision-making with advanced nature-inspired optimization provides a robust and efficient solution for next-generation industrial applications, paving the way for more intelligent, resilient, and resource-efficient IIoT systems.

items.title: A Large Language Model LLM Approach to COVID-19 Fake News Detection
items.abstract: Text classification is a widely studied problem in information retrieval and data mining, with applications ranging from healthcare diagnosis to the detection of COVID-19-related fake news. Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated text, and the rapid spread of misinformation during the pandemic has made automated fake news detection an important task. In this study, we apply pretrained transformer-based transfer learning (TL) models and large language models (LLMs), namely BERT-base, ALBERT-base, XLM-RoBERTa-base, DistilBERT, GPT-2, XLNet, and T5, to the COVID-19 English Tweets dataset, which contains 6,420 tweets labeled as real or fake. To further improve performance, we apply six late-fusion optimization techniques: weighted fusion, particle swarm optimization (PSO) fusion, the Nelder-Mead algorithm, Powell's method, the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm, and trust-region constrained optimization. Models are evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and confusion-matrix heatmaps are used to visualize the predictions of each model. GPT-2 achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 0.9631, precision of 0.9612, recall of 0.9610, and F1-score of 0.9600, while Nelder-Mead fusion achieved the best result among the fusion methods with an accuracy of 0.9610. These results highlight the value of LLMs for COVID-19 fake news detection. We conclude by outlining future directions, including multiclass classification, multilingual datasets, and real-time social media streams.

items.title: A Lifelong Neuro-Symbolic Explainable AI Twin for Zero-Touch 6G IoE Management Under Non-Stationary Network Dynamics
items.abstract: Future sixth-generation (6G) Internet of Everything (IoE) networks require zero-touch management systems capable of autonomously allocating communication and computational resources, satisfying service-level constraints, and providing transparent explanations for their decisions. Existing neuro-symbolic explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) twins improve interpretability by coupling neural prediction with symbolic reasoning; however, most rely on statically engineered causal graphs, fixed rule sets, and immutable knowledge bases. Such closed-world assumptions are unsuitable for non-stationary 6G environments in which radio conditions, mobility patterns, interference relationships, and service requirements continuously evolve. To address this limitation, this paper proposes LL-NS-XAI, a Lifelong Learning Neuro-Symbolic XAI Digital Twin for zero-touch 6G IoE management. The framework integrates three tightly coupled planes: an online implicit learner at the physical edge for time-varying service association and uplink/downlink resource allocation; a dynamic explicit learner in the virtual core for directed acyclic graph (DAG)-based Bayesian reasoning, most-probable-explanation inference, and explainable trust scoring; and a meta-cognitive layer that monitors reasoning residuals, detects parameter drift, structural drift, and ontological emergence, and autonomously revises the causal graph, probabilistic rule sets, conditional probability tables, and knowledge base. Unlike static neuro-symbolic twins, LL-NS-XAI treats realized post-decision outcomes, including achieved channel quality indicator (CQI), measured end-to-end delay, and throughput, as interventional evidence for online causal-model adaptation. Experimental evaluation using a non-stationary 5G-derived dataset with injected parameter drift, structural drift, and emergent IoE service classes demonstrates that LL-NS-XAI maintains higher long-term trustworthiness, lower reasoning residuals, and bounded performance degradation compared with static XAI twins, non-stationary bandits, and pure continual-learning baselines. The framework additionally accommodates a previously unseen IoE service class through autonomous causal-graph expansion, recovering near-oracle performance without offline retraining. These results demonstrate that lifelong causal adaptation can improve the robustness, explainability, and autonomy of AI-enabled zero-touch management in evolving 6G IoE networks.

items.title: A multi-stage validation framework for trustworthy large-scale clinical information extraction using large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise for extracting clinically meaningful information from unstructured health records, yet real-world deployment is constrained by limited scalable, trustworthy validation approaches. Conventional evaluation relies on annotation-intensive reference standards and incomplete structured data, limiting population-scale use. We propose a multi-stage validation framework for LLM-based clinical information extraction that enables rigorous assessment under weak supervision by integrating complementary validation strategies. The framework combines prompt calibration, rule-based filtering, semantic grounding, judge-LLM evaluation, expert review, and predictive validity analysis to quantify uncertainty without exhaustive manual annotation. We applied this framework to extract substance use disorder (SUD) diagnoses across 11 substance categories from 919,783 clinical notes. Rule-based filtering and semantic grounding removed 14.59% of LLM-positive extractions that were unsupported or structurally implausible. For high-uncertainty cases, the judge LLM showed substantial agreement with subject matter expert. Using judge evaluations as references, the primary LLM achieved an F1 score of 0.80. LLM-extracted SUD diagnoses predicted subsequent engagement in SUD specialty care more accurately than structured-data baselines. By unifying complementary validation strategies, this work presents a generalizable human-in-the-loop framework for establishing the trustworthiness of LLM-based clinical information extraction at scale while minimizing the need for exhaustive manual annotation.
